summary: On a mountain in Galilee the risen Jesus claims all authority, sends His disciples to make disciples of all nations, and promises to be with them always.
key_insight: Matthew does not hide that “some doubted,” even as they worshiped. Jesus did not wait until every doubt was gone. He “came and spoke to them,” and gave His commission to worshipers with doubts still among them.
story: The eleven disciples went away into Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had appointed for them. When they saw Him, they worshiped Him; but some doubted. {Mt}

Jesus came and spoke to them: “All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you; and lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” {Mt}

Mark gives the commission in other words: “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned.” Signs would follow those who believe. In His name they would cast out demons and speak with new tongues; they would take up serpents, drink anything deadly without harm, and lay hands on the sick, who would recover. {Mk}
Paul records that, after appearing to Peter and the Twelve, Jesus “was seen by over five hundred brethren at once,” most of whom were still living when he wrote. He does not say where it happened.
differences: Matthew names the setting, a mountain in Galilee, and notes that some doubted. Mark gives no setting beyond placing these words after the appearance at the table (16:14).
Matthew’s commission centers on making disciples, baptizing and teaching. Mark’s centers on preaching the gospel to every creature.
Only Matthew records the claim to “all authority,” the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and the promise “I am with you always.” Only Mark lists the signs that would follow believers.
Neither Gospel mentions the five hundred; only Paul does (1 Corinthians 15:6).

fit.question: Matthew speaks of the eleven on the mountain in Galilee. Paul says Jesus was seen by more than five hundred at once. Were these the same appearance?

points.label: A meeting announced ahead
points.text: Jesus had sent word through the women for His brethren to go to Galilee (28:10), and the place was set in advance (28:16). A gathering announced beforehand, in the region where most of His followers lived, would explain how five hundred could be together at once. McGarvey took this view, and Edersheim also placed the appearance to the five hundred in Galilee.

points.label: Who doubted?
points.text: If a larger crowd was there, “some doubted” may describe some who were seeing Him for the first time. It may also mean hesitation among the eleven themselves. Matthew does not say.

points.label: Two occasions
points.text: Others think Paul’s five hundred saw Jesus on a different occasion. Matthew mentions only the eleven, and Paul gives neither a place nor a time.

fit.note: Matthew and Paul may describe the same day or two different ones. Either way, they agree that the risen Jesus was seen by many people, not by a few.
fit.short: Many think the five hundred gathered at this announced meeting in Galilee. Matthew names only the eleven, and Paul gives no place.

fit.question: In Mark, “Go into all the world” follows directly after Jesus appears to the eleven at the table (16:14–15), which sounds like Jerusalem on Resurrection Sunday. Matthew sets the commission on a mountain in Galilee. Which is it?

points.label: Mark’s summary moves quickly
points.text: Mark 16:9–20 covers many appearances in a few verses. “And He said to them” joins sayings without marking time. Mark then says Jesus was received up “after the Lord had spoken to them” (16:19), though Acts says the appearances lasted forty days (Acts 1:3).

points.label: A mission given more than once
points.text: Jesus spoke of the mission on several occasions: on Resurrection Sunday evening (John 20:21), on the mountain in Galilee (Matthew 28:19), and in Jerusalem before the ascension (Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8). Mark gathers its substance in one place.

fit.note: A short summary that passes over time is not an error. Luke’s Gospel does the same, and Luke himself supplies the timing in Acts.
fit.short: Mark’s brief summary joins sayings without marking time. Jesus spoke of the mission several times, in Jerusalem and in Galilee.

scene.label: All the nations
scene.text: The word for nations is the usual word for Gentiles. Earlier Jesus had sent the Twelve only to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 10:6). Now the field is the world, as God had promised Abraham that in him “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3).

scene.label: Living witnesses
scene.text: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians about twenty-five years after the resurrection. By noting that most of the five hundred were still alive, he was in effect saying that his readers could still ask them.

scene.label: Believing and baptism
scene.text: Mark’s words join believing and baptism, but the condemnation falls on the one who “does not believe.” Christians differ on what baptism does and on whether it is for infants or only for believers. All agree that baptism belongs to the commission and that saving faith is necessary.

scene.label: The signs
scene.text: Acts shows most of them: a demon cast out (Acts 16:18), new tongues (Acts 2:4), Paul unharmed by a viper (Acts 28:3–6), and the sick healed by the laying on of hands (Acts 28:8). Nothing here commands handling snakes as a test of faith. Christians differ on how far such signs continue today.

scene.label: The manuscripts
scene.text: Mark’s form of the commission comes from Mark 16:9–20. The NKJV includes these verses and notes that some of the oldest manuscripts lack them.

witnesses.matthew: Matthew ends his Gospel on this mountain, with the King claiming all authority and sending His people to all nations. The Gospel that opened with “Immanuel,” God with us (1:23), closes with “I am with you always.” Matthew’s story often turns on mountains, from the Sermon on the Mount (5:1) to this last word.
witnesses.mark: Mark’s longer ending gives the commission its widest reach: “all the world” and “every creature.” Salvation is joined to believing, and the promised signs are not displays for their own sake but the Lord’s way of confirming the preached word, as Mark’s closing verse says (16:20).

seeing.reveals: Jesus reigns now with all authority in heaven and on earth. He uses that authority to send His followers to every nation and to stay with them every day until the end.
seeing.living: The commission was given to worshipers who still had doubts, and its promise covers every day of the work: “I am with you always.” Jesus asks for disciples, people baptized and taught to obey Him, not only converts. Ask where He is sending you to help someone follow Him, and lean on His presence more than your own certainty.
seeing.ponder: Who is one person Jesus may be asking you to help become His disciple, and what keeps you from trusting His promise to be with you?

preaching.big_idea: With all authority, Jesus sends us to all nations, and He is with us all the days.
outline: The promise: I am with you (20b)
preaching.watch_for: Count the word “all”: all authority, all the nations, all things, and “always,” which in Greek is literally all the days (28:18–20). The mission rests on Jesus’ authority at the start and Jesus’ presence at the end.

title: The Great Commission
